newsitem.title: USA: Dole calls for postponement of Bosnian elections.
newsitem.headline: Dole calls for postponement of Bosnian elections.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole repeated his criticism of the planned Bosnian elections on Thursday in the city where they were conceived, and called on President Bill Clinton to postpone them.

Dole, who condemned the elections in a statement last week, sought to dramatise his position by repeating it during a campaign trip to the industrial city where the Bosnian peace accords were negotiated last year.

"These elections make a mockery of our principles and commitment to democracy," Dole said. "There is still time for the president to postpone these elections. Many Americans, regardless of party, think it's a big mistake to pursue what would in effect be sham elections."
"These elections will be a fraud, but a fraud with the American stamp of approval," he added.

The Republican candidate, who trails Clinton by 15 to 20 percentage points in opinion polls, last week wrote to the president urging him to put off the Bosnian elections, scheduled to take place on Sept. 14.
"The conditions for free and fair elections do not exist," Dole said on Thursday. "War criminals are not just roaming free, some are even on the ballot."

Elections for president and several legislative chambers are being run by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. The Dayton treaty says the elections, which are supposed to reunify the ethnically divided country, should be "free and fair."
But human rights workers say the voter registration process was plagued by abuses and nationalist authorities have stifled free speech and free movement.
James Rubin, the foreign policy spokesman for the Clinton-Gore campaign, acknowledged that the conditions for holding the election may not be ideal but argued that the vote should still take place.
"It is going to be a long time before there are perfect conditions in Bosnia for elections, but in order to continue to move from war to peace ... the elections have to go forward," Rubin said.
"The elections are the beginning, not the end, of what is going to be a very long-term process of democratization in Bosina," added a U.S. official who asked not to be named.
Clinton has promised to bring some 20,000 U.S. troops home after they finish their one-year mission in December as part of the NATO-led peace force.
